description: Comparing one democratic and one non-democratic political system beyond the UK.
content_html:
Why Compare How Countries Are Governed?

Understanding how other countries govern themselves helps citizens evaluate the strengths and weaknesses of their own political system. It also reveals that representative democracy — the system used in the UK, where citizens elect representatives to make decisions on their behalf — is not the only way a state can organise its political life. Comparing a democratic system with a non-democratic one illustrates what is at stake when governments do or do not allow citizens to participate freely.

Example of a Democratic System: The United States of America

The United States operates a federal system of government, meaning political power is divided between the national (federal) government in Washington DC and the fifty individual state governments. At the federal level, law-making power rests with Congress, which is bicameral — it has two chambers, the Senate and the House of Representatives. Executive power is held by the President, who is both head of state and head of government, elected separately from Congress through a system involving an Electoral College.

Citizens in the USA can vote in presidential elections, congressional elections, senate elections, and many state and local elections. They also have constitutional protections for individual rights through the Bill of Rights, which includes freedoms of speech, the press, religion and assembly. The judiciary is independent of the executive and legislature, with the Supreme Court able to strike down laws that violate the Constitution.

However, the USA’s democratic system has also faced challenges. Voter turnout in many elections is lower than in comparable democracies. The Electoral College system has on several occasions produced a President who received fewer total votes than their main opponent — a feature that some critics argue undermines equal representation, while supporters argue it protects the interests of smaller states and maintains the federal balance of power.

Key Fact

In the USA, political power is divided between a federal government and fifty state governments. Congress (the legislature) is bicameral: the Senate and the House of Representatives. The President holds executive power and is elected separately, not as leader of the largest party in Congress. Citizens have constitutional rights protected by the Bill of Rights and enforced by an independent Supreme Court.

Both the UK and the USA hold regular free elections, have independent judiciaries, protect civil liberties, and operate bicameral legislatures. However, there are significant structural differences. The UK has a constitutional monarchy with a Prime Minister who leads the party (or coalition) with the most seats in the House of Commons and can therefore be removed by Parliament. The USA has an elected President who serves a fixed four-year term regardless of congressional support. The UK constitution is uncodified (not written in a single document), while the US Constitution is a single written document with formal amendment procedures. The UK’s House of Lords is unelected; both chambers of the US Congress are elected.

Example of a Non-Democratic System: The People’s Republic of China

The People’s Republic of China is governed by the Chinese Communist Party (CCP), which has been the sole governing party since 1949. China’s political system does not allow for multi-party elections at a national level: citizens cannot vote to remove the governing party or choose between competing parties for national leadership. The National People’s Congress formally enacts laws, but political authority in practice flows from the CCP’s leadership structure rather than from elected representatives chosen through free competition.

Freedoms of speech, the press, and assembly that are protected in democratic systems are significantly restricted in China. Independent journalism, opposition political activity, and online expression on politically sensitive topics are subject to legal restrictions and censorship. This means that citizens have limited formal mechanisms to challenge government decisions, hold leaders to account, or advocate for change through channels outside the party structure.

It is important to note that there are different perspectives on how to evaluate China’s political system. The government of China argues that its system delivers stability, long-term economic planning, and the rapid lifting of hundreds of millions of people out of poverty. It contends that Western democratic models are not universally superior and that different cultures and histories lead to different legitimate forms of governance. Critics — including international human rights organisations and many democratic governments — argue that without free elections and independent media, citizens cannot hold their government accountable, and that political rights are fundamental to human dignity.

Key Fact

China is governed by one political party (the Chinese Communist Party) without multi-party national elections. Political freedoms including free speech, a free press, and political opposition are significantly restricted. In contrast, citizens in democratic systems such as the USA or UK can vote in competitive elections, form and join opposition parties, and access independent media.

One viewpoint holds that democratic systems, despite their imperfections, are fundamentally superior because they allow citizens to remove governments they disagree with, protect minority rights through an independent judiciary, and ensure accountability through a free press. Organisations such as Freedom House, which monitors civil and political rights internationally, classify democratic participation as a core human right.

A contrasting viewpoint holds that different societies have different political traditions, needs and priorities, and that a government that delivers economic development, security and social stability may command genuine popular support without fitting the Western democratic template. Some political scientists argue that democratic forms alone do not guarantee justice or equality, pointing to examples of democratic states that have nonetheless failed to protect minorities or address economic inequality effectively.

Students should be aware that comparing political systems is a contested academic and political exercise, and that terms like “democracy” are themselves sometimes disputed. For exam purposes, the key is to present both viewpoints fairly and use specific evidence from both systems.
exam_tip_html: For an 8-mark “Analyse” or 12-mark “Evaluate” question on how other countries are governed, a very common mistake is writing a vague comparison that does not name either country specifically or describe their actual features. Examiners reward answers that name the specific country, describe two or three concrete features of its system, and compare those features to the UK or to a contrasting system. Avoid value judgements that read as politically biased: write “critics argue that” or “supporters of this system contend that” rather than asserting one system is simply better. For the 12-mark Evaluate, you must reach a substantiated judgement — weigh the evidence and explain your conclusion. Simply listing facts about two countries without evaluation does not access the highest marks.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The USA is an example of a democratic federal system with a bicameral legislature (Congress), an elected President, a written constitution and independent judiciary, and citizens protected by the Bill of Rights. It differs from the UK in having an elected rather than appointed upper chamber, a written constitution, and a separately elected executive.
  • China is an example of a non-democratic system in which the Chinese Communist Party governs without multi-party national elections, and freedoms of speech, the press, and political opposition are significantly restricted.
  • Comparing systems involves presenting multiple viewpoints: supporters of China’s system point to stability and economic development; critics argue that without free elections citizens cannot hold governments accountable. Exam questions require you to present both sides and reach a substantiated conclusion.

practice_questions.text:
The legislature of the United States is called:
A) The Senate
B) Parliament
C) Congress
D) The Cabinet
Identify two ways in which citizens in a democratic system can participate in politics that citizens in a non-democratic system typically cannot.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for each clearly distinct way, up to 2 marks. Acceptable answers include: voting in free and fair competitive elections; forming or joining opposition political parties; accessing independent media; protesting or demonstrating freely; criticising the government in public without fear of prosecution. Two versions of the same point (e.g. 'vote' and 'go to the polls') score only 1 mark.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the political system in the United States of America.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks: 2 marks per feature (1 for identifying the feature, 1 for developing it). Example: the USA uses a federal system of government (1 mark), meaning power is divided between a national federal government and fifty individual state governments (1 mark). The USA has a bicameral legislature called Congress (1 mark), consisting of two chambers: the Senate and the House of Representatives (1 mark). Other valid features include the separately elected President, the Bill of Rights, or the independent Supreme Court. Answers must describe rather than evaluate.

practice_questions.text:
Read the extract below and answer the question that follows.

A fictional international affairs research centre published the following findings in a 2024 briefing:

‘In a survey of 3,200 adults across twelve countries, 71% of respondents in established democratic states said they felt able to criticise their government without fear of personal consequences. In states classified as non-democratic by Freedom House, this figure fell to 18%. Of those in non-democratic states who said they felt unable to speak out, 64% identified fear of legal consequences as the primary barrier.’

Using the extract and your own knowledge, what does this source suggest about the difference between democratic and non-democratic political systems?
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks: 1 mark for identifying what the source shows (a stark difference in citizens' freedom to criticise government between democratic and non-democratic states); 1 mark for interpreting the significance (the 18% figure in non-democratic states suggests political freedom is severely curtailed and that legal consequences deter participation); 1 mark for applying own knowledge (linking to features of non-democratic systems such as China's restrictions on free speech, press censorship, or the absence of multi-party elections); 1 mark for a substantiated judgement combining source and own knowledge (e.g. the source suggests that the absence of free speech fundamentally undermines accountability, because if citizens cannot criticise government without fear, governments cannot be effectively held to account).

practice_questions.text: Analyse the key differences between a democratic and a non-democratic political system, using one example of each type of system.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sustained analysis that breaks down the comparison into specific features (elections, civil liberties, rule of law, accountability, freedom of press), names at least one concrete example from each system (e.g. the USA's Bill of Rights or Congress vs China's single-party governance or press restrictions), weighs evidence on both sides, and reaches a substantiated judgement about which features are most important for democratic accountability.

Secure: Covers both democratic and non-democratic features with some development and at least one named real-world example from each system. A judgement is reached, though the analysis may not be fully sustained.

Developing: Relevant points about both systems but limited development; may list features without analysing them or name only one system specifically.

Emerging: Basic description of democracy vs non-democracy with little development; no named real-world examples; no analytical judgement.

practice_questions.text:
A school citizenship debate is considering the motion: ‘Democratic systems are always better for citizens than non-democratic ones.’

Evaluate this statement, referring to one democratic and one non-democratic political system outside the UK.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Full two-sided argument with multiple developed points for and against the motion; names at least one specific real-world example per side (e.g. the USA's Bill of Rights, Congress, and Electoral College debates on the democratic side; China's single-party governance, restrictions on free speech, and economic development argument on the non-democratic side); reaches a substantiated overall judgement that weighs the evidence and explains why one position is stronger.

Secure: Both sides presented with at least one named real-world example; a conclusion is reached, but the evaluative judgement may lack full justification.

Developing: Relevant points on both sides but limited development; argument may be mainly one-sided; examples may be vague ('some democratic countries').

Emerging: Basic points about democracy with little development; no named real-world examples from outside the UK; no substantiated conclusion.

Content that could be credited — Arguments in support: free elections allow citizens to remove governments they disagree with; an independent judiciary protects individual rights; freedom of the press ensures accountability; the USA's Bill of Rights is a model of constitutionally protected rights. Arguments against: democratic systems can fail to protect minorities or reduce inequality; some non-democratic governments claim to command genuine popular support; China's government points to economic development and stability as benefits; different historical and cultural contexts mean democracy may not function the same way in every society.

knowledge_checks.q: What term describes a system of government where power is divided between a national government and regional state governments?
Which of the following best describes the political system of China?
options: A federal democratic republic with free elections
A constitutional monarchy with a Prime Minister
A single-party state governed by the Chinese Communist Party
A parliamentary democracy with proportional representation

knowledge_checks.q: The US legislature, called Congress, is _____ because it has two chambers: the Senate and the House of Representatives.
In the USA, the constitutional rights of citizens are protected by the _____ of Rights, which includes freedoms of speech, religion, and assembly.
Match each political feature to the country it best describes:

flashcard_questions.a: A system where citizens elect representatives to make decisions on their behalf.

flashcard_questions.q: What is a federal system of government?
flashcard_questions.a: Political power is divided between a central national government and regional state governments.

flashcard_questions.q: What does 'bicameral' mean in the context of a legislature?
flashcard_questions.a: Consisting of two separate chambers, each with different roles in the law-making process.

flashcard_questions.q: What are the two chambers of the US Congress?
flashcard_questions.a: The Senate and the House of Representatives.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the Bill of Rights in the USA?
flashcard_questions.a: A set of constitutional amendments protecting freedoms of speech, religion, press and assembly.

flashcard_questions.q: How is the US President elected?
flashcard_questions.a: Separately from Congress through a system involving an Electoral College.

flashcard_questions.q: Which party has governed China since 1949?
Name one political freedom significantly restricted in China compared to democratic systems.
flashcard_questions.a: Freedom of the press (independent journalism is subject to restrictions and censorship).

flashcard_questions.q: What argument do supporters of China's political system often make about its governance?
flashcard_questions.a: That it delivers stability, long-term economic planning, and rapid reduction in poverty.

flashcard_questions.q: What argument do critics make about non-democratic political systems?
flashcard_questions.a: Without free elections, citizens cannot hold governments accountable.

flashcard_questions.q: How does the US Constitution differ from the UK constitution?
flashcard_questions.a: The US Constitution is a single written document; the UK's is uncodified (not written in one document).

flashcard_questions.q: What is the role of the US Supreme Court in relation to the Constitution?
flashcard_questions.a: It can strike down laws that violate the Constitution, acting as a check on government power.

glossary_terms.definition: A system of government in which power is held by elected representatives chosen through free and fair elections by citizens.
A system of government in which power is divided between a central national government and regional state governments, each with defined areas of authority.
Consisting of two separate chambers or houses, each with different roles in the law-making process.
The principle that the powers of government should be divided between separate institutions — typically the legislature, executive and judiciary — so that no single branch holds unchecked authority.

The system used in US presidential elections in which voters choose state electors who then formally cast votes for president, meaning the winner must secure a majority of electoral votes rather than the national popular vote.
A system of rule in which power is concentrated in a leader or small group, political opposition is suppressed and citizens have little meaningful ability to participate in or change the government.

items.title: The Bunker: Inside Authoritarian States
items.description: Journalism-led podcast examining how authoritarian governments maintain power and how citizens respond. Provides balanced, evidence-based analysis of non-democratic systems.

items.title: Political Thinking with Nick Robinson: Comparing Democracies
items.description: Nick Robinson interviews politicians and political scientists about how different countries structure their governments, with regular comparisons to the UK system.

items.title: Justice: What's the Right Thing to Do? Episode 1 — Harvard University
items.description: Michael Sandel's celebrated Harvard course on justice and political philosophy. Episode 1 introduces the fundamental question of how governments should weigh individual rights against collective benefit.

items.title: The Moral Roots of Liberals and Conservatives — Jonathan Haidt (TED)
items.description: Haidt explains why people across different political cultures hold fundamentally different values — essential context for understanding why democratic and non-democratic systems attract genuine popular support.

items.title: The Danger of a Single Story — Chimamanda Ngozi Adichie (TED)
items.description: Adichie's acclaimed TED talk on how relying on a single narrative distorts our understanding of other peoples and countries. Essential for avoiding simplistic comparisons of political systems.

items.title: 13th (2016)
items.description: Ava DuVernay's documentary exploring race, justice and democracy in the USA through the lens of the 13th Amendment. Shows strengths and limitations of the American democratic system.

items.title: The Trial of the Chicago 7 (2020)
items.description: Aaron Sorkin's acclaimed film dramatising a landmark US trial that tested the boundaries of free speech, protest rights and judicial independence — all key features of democratic systems.

items.title: BBC Bitesize: Comparing Political Systems
items.description: GCSE Citizenship revision on democratic and non-democratic systems, with examples, key terms and practice questions.

items.title: Freedom House: Freedom in the World Annual Report
items.description: Freedom House publishes annual scores for political rights and civil liberties in every country. Use the country profiles to compare the USA, China and the UK against objective criteria.

items.title: UK Parliament: Democracy Around the World — Education Resource
items.description: Parliament's education service resource comparing different forms of government, designed specifically for secondary school citizenship students.
